To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
gold (III )porphyrin  1a preferentially induces apoptosis in a cancer cell line (SUNE 1).
gold (III)-based drugs induce apoptosis through multiple pathways in cancer cells.
gold (III)-porphyrin 2a induced cell death by activating multiple pathways and the balance between pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic signals determined cell fate in SUNE1 cancer cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new gold anticancer drug and provides a new approach for the study of the molecular mechanisms of metal anticancer drugs
the molecular mechanisms of the cytotoxicity of gold (III)-based anticancer drugs,
the mechanism of gold (I) porphyrins as a new class of metal‐based anticancer drug.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
gold (III)-porphyrin 2a induced apoptosis through the mitochondrial pathway in SUNE1 cancer cells, and this cytotoxicity is related to multiple factors.
gold (III)-based anticancer drugs may be a promising new generation of anticancer drugs.
the gold (III) complex 1a induced cell death in SUNE1 cancer cells via a mechanism that is distinct from that induced by cisplatin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
gold (III)-containing complexes are a new class of potential anticancer drug candidates.

the cytotoxic action of gold (III)-porphyrin 4a was mainly mediated by the mitochondrial apoptosis pathway, which was triggered by the generation of ROS, the inhibition of the translation process and the activation of the autophagy‐lysosome pathway.
gold (III)-porphyrin 3a induced apoptosis in cancer cells by affecting the expression of multiple proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
gold (III)-based anticancer drugs may have the potential to be developed as a promising anticancer therapy.
gold (III)-containing complexes are potential anticancer drugs with high selectivity for cancer cells and low toxicity.
the proteomic approach is a useful method for identifying the molecular targets of metal complexes and can help in the development of new metal anticancer drugs.
